article.title: When More Data Makes a Bad Estimate More Convincing
article.why: Practical analytical English with higher-difficulty emphasis.

paragraphs.en:
Large datasets reduce random sampling error, but they do not automatically make an estimate correct. This distinction matters because modern analytics teams can work with millions of records and still produce highly precise answers to the wrong question. More data can make a biased estimate look more convincing by shrinking its standard error while leaving the underlying bias untouched.

Selection bias is one common example. Suppose an online survey receives responses from 500,000 users, but only highly engaged app users are invited to participate. The sample is enormous, so the estimated satisfaction rate may have a very narrow confidence interval. Yet the estimate may still fail to represent occasional users, customers who disabled notifications, or people who stopped using the app. The uncertainty reported by the confidence interval captures random variation under the sampling model; it does not automatically capture the systematic exclusion of important groups.

Measurement error creates a similar problem. If a sensor is consistently miscalibrated, collecting one billion readings will estimate the wrong value with extraordinary precision. In business data, definitions can play the role of a miscalibrated instrument. A ‘customer’ table that silently excludes cash-only buyers or a ‘conversion’ label that misses offline purchases can create stable but biased measurements. Large sample size does not repair the definition.

Causal analysis adds another layer. A huge observational dataset can reveal very stable correlations, but confounding does not disappear because N is large. If customers who receive a premium service are already wealthier, more loyal, or more active, millions of rows may estimate that association very precisely without identifying the causal effect of the service. Precision answers ‘how much random uncertainty remains under these assumptions?’ Identification asks whether the assumptions let us learn the quantity we actually care about.

This is why analysts should distinguish variance, bias, and model misspecification. More observations usually reduce variance. Better sampling design, measurement design, and causal assumptions are needed to address other errors. Data quality reviews should therefore ask how the population was formed, how variables were measured, which cases were excluded, and what process assigned treatments or exposures.

The practical danger is rhetorical. A result based on ten million rows sounds authoritative, and dashboards can display many decimal places. But a narrow interval around a biased number is not strong evidence about the target population. Scale is valuable only when the data-generating process supports the intended conclusion. Good analysis uses large data to increase information, not to substitute for design. Statistical significance can amplify this problem. With a very large sample, tiny differences become statistically significant even when they are practically unimportant or generated by bias. A difference of 0.05 percentage points may produce a microscopic p-value if the dataset contains tens of millions of observations. That calculation says little about whether the difference matters to customers, whether it will replicate under a new policy, or whether the comparison is fair.

Representativeness is also not a simple function of sample size. A carefully drawn sample of a few thousand people can estimate a population quantity better than millions of convenience observations. Historical examples in survey research show that coverage and nonresponse can dominate raw sample count. Digital products face modern versions of the same problem: telemetry often represents users who consented, stayed online, used supported devices, or survived long enough to generate events.

Analysts should therefore report both scale and design. Saying ‘N = 8 million’ is useful, but it should be accompanied by the target population, inclusion rules, missingness, measurement definitions, and known sources of selection. Precision should be interpreted conditionally on those choices. The bigger the dataset, the easier it becomes to forget that the rows did not appear by magic; they were produced by a product, policy, instrumentation system, and set of eligibility rules.
paragraphs.zh:
【重點翻譯】大樣本主要能降低 random sampling error，卻不會自動消除 selection bias、measurement error 或錯誤的 causal assumption。若一份問卷只邀請高度活躍的 app 使用者，即使回收 50 萬份，信賴區間可以非常窄，但它仍可能無法代表低頻使用者或已流失者。這時『很精準』只是表示在既定 sampling model 下隨機誤差小，不代表估計對 target population 無偏。

measurement error 也是如此：若感測器固定偏高，收集十億筆資料只會非常精準地估錯。因果分析更明顯：N 很大可以把 correlation 估得很穩，但 confounding 不會因此消失。大型資料集甚至容易讓極小、沒有商業意義的差異變成統計顯著。

因此分析要分清 variance、bias 與 model misspecification。除了 N，還要報告 population、inclusion rule、missingness、measurement definition 與 selection mechanism。資料很多不是設計正確的替代品。
paragraphs.ja:
【重点訳】大規模dataが主に減らすのはrandom sampling errorであり、selection bias、measurement error、誤ったcausal assumptionを自動的に修正するわけではない。appのheavy userだけにsurveyを送れば、50万件の回答があってもtarget populationを代表しない可能性がある。confidence intervalが狭いことは、設定したsampling modelの下でrandom uncertaintyが小さいことを示すだけで、systematic biasが小さいことを保証しない。

同様に、常にずれたsensorから10億件集めれば『非常に精密な誤答』になる。causal analysisでも、Nが大きくなってもconfoundingは消えない。したがってvariance、bias、model misspecificationを分け、population、inclusion rule、measurement definition、selection mechanismまで確認する必要がある。

vocabulary.usage: Random uncertainty reduced by larger samples.
Systematic mismatch between sample and target population.
Error created by how variables are measured.
Describes uncertainty under a statistical model.
A causal threat that sample size alone does not remove.
Using an incorrect model or data-generating assumption.
Whether the sample reflects the intended population.
Who has a chance to enter the data.
Describes the persuasive appearance of very large datasets.

business.term: Large N does not repair a biased design.
business.explanation: 大樣本不能修正有偏的設計。

business.term: Report both scale and data-generating process.
business.explanation: 同時報告資料規模與產生機制。
